text:
Happy Friday! The leftover snow from the overnight system is done, and we're left with a gray, cloudy day with a high near 41. Tonight stays cloudy, down to around 29, and a few snow showers could start after 5 in the morning.

Saturday is the wet one. Every model I look at has it, and the forecasters agree. Showers of rain mixed with wet snow build in by late morning, with the best odds from noon to about 4, when the chance runs better than 60 percent. The high is near 42, but it will feel colder inside a shower, and a burst of graupel or wet snow is possible even down here. Amounts are light, just a few hundredths of an inch of water, and nothing sticks in town. The showers linger into the evening, with a low near 30.

Sunday starts with snow showers likely before 8, then a mix of rain and snow showers until about 1. After that it tapers off and is done by evening. It stays mostly cloudy with a high near 42, and the amounts are even lighter than Saturday's.

The pattern flips next week. Forecasters have high confidence in dry weather, with sunshine returning Monday and highs in the low to mid 40s, climbing toward the 50s by midweek.

Saturday morning is your dry window. Keep a hood or umbrella handy from late morning on.

week.blurb: Cloudy and chilly all day with a high near 41, staying dry until a few snow flakes are possible before dawn Saturday.
A gray, damp Saturday with rain and snow showers on and off, a high near 42, nothing sticking, so grab the umbrella.
Leftover rain and snow showers taper off around 1, then it's mostly cloudy with a high near 42, so the afternoon is your window.
Looks like mostly sunny skies return Monday, a touch warmer with a high near 44, though the night turns frosty near 26.
Sunny and milder Tuesday, with a high near 49 and a pretty good bet for a long walk.
Trending mostly sunny and a little warmer again Wednesday, with a high near 51 and a mild south breeze.
If the pattern holds, Thursday stays mostly sunny and dry with a high near 52, a gentle finish to the week.

AFD KEY MESSAGES (forecaster's reasoning, issued 2026-11-13T06:49:00+00:00 — covers the whole BTV area, northern NY included: translate to what Burlington feels, never repeat other regions' place names):
  1. Lingering snow ends early this morning.
  2. Widespread upslope snow showers Saturday, gradually tapering off Sunday.
  3. High confidence for dry weather and above normal temperatures next week.
AFD WHAT CHANGED (same regional caveat): As of 149 AM EST Friday... No significant changes.
AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: The center of the surface low has passed slightly to the east and backside cold air advection is causing the lingering rain to gradually change to snow. Snow levels have dropped to the valley floors in the Southern Champlain Valley and Marble Valley around and south of Rutland. However, snow levels are slightly higher east of the Greens as some of the surface cold air advection is being blocked, so they still range around 750 ft. So far, 1-3 inches looks to have fallen above 1500 ft in the southern Greens and the surfaces of the mountain passes have begun to become snow covered. Within the next couple hours, snow levels should reach the Connecticut River but the precipitation will end shortly after. Additional accumulations between 1-2 inches are possible around and above 1,000 ft while mostly just a slushy coating is expected below. Precipitation will end by around 8 AM. KEY MESSAGE 2: For the weekend, cyclonic northwest flow will prevail under an upper level low. However, for today, the region will be in an area of subsidence between shortwaves so it will be mostly dry, though a couple upslope flurries will be possible in the mountains. A potent embedded shortwave will pass south tomorrow and tomorrow night, bringing widespread showers. While they will be most concentrated in the typical northwest flow upslope areas, very marginal instability will develop in the lower 10,000 ft in the atmosphere due to cold air aloft and solar heating. This will cause the precipitation to trend more convective, especially Saturday afternoon. Therefore, snow showers will be able to survive crossing the terrain and should pass through the downslope areas like the Connecticut River Valley, though likely in a lighter form. While temperatures will rise above freezing below 2,000 ft, and likely reach 40 in the lowest points, temperatures will drop significantly in any of the showers. Therefore, even though consistent snow levels will likely only be down to around 1,000-1,500 ft, a period of graupel or even brief wet snow will be possible all the way down into the valleys. However, any continuous accumulations should generally be limited to above 2,000 ft. The showers will gradually become less and less widespread heading into Sunday, and they should be done by Sunday evening. Accumulations by the end should be in the 1-4 inch range above 2,500 ft, with mostly brief coatings that melt below that. The lowest accumulating snow will fall Saturday night. Moisture off Lake Champlain will enhance the showers in the parts of the Champlain Valley and Greens, but the more convective nature may prevent the formation of distinct bands. KEY MESSAGE 3: Deterministic and ensemble guidance are in strong agreement that an 2-3 standard deviation ridge of high pressure will be centered to the south and west of the North Country next week. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Friday! Any leftover snow showers across central and southern parts of the area are quickly wrapping up through the mid to late morning. We are left dry, but cloudy through the rest of the day ahead. Temperatures for the day will head back into the upper 30s and lower 40s by this afternoon. Tonight mainly cloudy skies stick around as overnight lows fall into the 30s. This weekend stays gray, cloudy, and a bit unsettled. Clouds stay pretty stubborn as we continue to see valley rain showers and mountain snow showers. This time it will be the mountains of the northern half of the area that seem to be the big winner. Through Saturday and Sunday the mountain peaks north could run upwards of 6″ of new snow. Just like the last system, this will be highly elevation dependent, and as you get below the summits the snow totals drop off very quickly. I am not anticipating many issues on the roads, but some of the mountain passes could become slick from time to time. Temperatures both days are generally in the upper 30s to the lower 40s. We flip a switch into next week as sunshine tries to start to make an appearance into the day Monday. Temperatures are still on the cooler side to start the week in the low to mid 40s. Sunshine continues through Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of next week. With all the sunshine we’ll see temperatures head back towards the low and mid 50s by midweek.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-13T00:00:00Z — same caveat): Slippery travel early in southern Vermont, cloudy Friday afternoon — Rain and elevation snow will wrap up Friday morning. Some roads will be slippery, either from frozen standing water, or snow accumulation. Mountain towns will experience more of this. Little to no precipitation is expected north of Burlington through Friday morning. Several inches of snow will fall in southern parts of the region, higher up. The weekend brings more clouds with persistent rain and snow showers. Snow accumulation is expected in the northern mountains over the weekend. Drier and brighter weather is likely next week, followed by a warmup into the 50s.
